docs.title: Author or update a DDD
docs.text:
1. Start with DDD source formats to understand the domain, ontology, and service-interface components.
  2. Choose Domain XML or DDD JSON.
  3. Look up domain declarations and plan items to define dialogue behavior.
  4. Define vocabulary in the ontology and application operations in the Service Interface.

Treat the cross-repository interfaces as coordinated revision contracts, not as implied compatibility from those individual version identifiers.

docs.title: Runtime architecture
docs.text:
The current runtime has two HTTP boundaries that serve different callers:

  1. The Handler accepts application interaction requests.
  2. The Pipeline coordinates dialogue-processing services for the Handler.

Tala supplies DDD loading, shared semantic models, and authored NLG realization. TDM's Dialogue Management Engine (DME) updates the dialogue state and selects moves from those models. NLU/NDU and NDG services participate in interpretation and realization. The Pipeline also performs Tala's in-process NLG realization and coordinates calls according to the request, session, configured endpoints, and enabled neural settings.

docs.title: Request path
docs.text:
Application
    │ interaction request
    ▼
Handler (/interact/{offer_id})
    │ prepares offer/session and forwards request
    ▼
Pipeline (route `pipeline-fn`; direct path `/api/pipeline-fn` by default)
    ├── language understanding and interpretation
    ├── DME dialogue processing
    ├── optional follow-up component calls
    └── response enrichment
    │
    ▼
Handler response to application

The Handler may load an offer when the session does not already contain its ODB. An existing session.offer_id takes precedence over the route's offer_id; changing the route while continuing an existing session does not switch offers. The Handler forwards the request to the Pipeline, handles any service invocation requested by the Pipeline, and resubmits the result until a user-facing response is ready. It also applies Handler-specific behavior such as session encryption, wakeword handling, and response timing.

The Pipeline's request runner prepares session data, coordinates interpretation and DME processing, may restart interpretation after an ASR/NDU correction, then enriches the response and trims dialogue history. It invokes NLG through Tala in-process; NLG is not a separately configured FUNCTION_ENDPOINT_* service. This is asynchronous service orchestration, not a single direct DME call.

docs.title: Revision and compatibility boundary
docs.text:
Implementation details in this reference correspond to these source revisions: Handler 44616a5e34b6, Pipeline 34c971f1aef8, TDM f555673fec31, and Tala 31.0.2 source commit bc6f9cbabf81. These identify the documented source baselines, not necessarily the deployed revisions. The Handler version cited here registers only /interact/{offer_id}; wakeword handling occurs within that route and does not create a separate legacy interact route. Check deployment revisions before relying on implementation-specific details.

The Handler, Pipeline, and TDM versions cited above have service-continuation contract mismatches. In particular, Handler action/validator result payloads do not match TDM's declared request schema, and Pipeline's service-result guard expects an event marker that Handler's continuation does not add. Service action and validator round-trips are therefore not compatible across these specific revisions; see the API pages for details.

docs.title: Handler interaction API
docs.text: The Handler is the application-facing runtime boundary. The Handler version documented here registers the route interact/{offer_id} (with an empty Functions route prefix). It does not register a legacy interact route. The production client contract uses the TDM interaction request envelope.

docs.title: Request envelope
docs.text:
The request is JSON with a version, session, and request operation. For example, a session-start request has this shape:

{
  "version": "3.4",
  "session": {},
  "request": {
    "start_session": {}
  }
}

Natural-language input is represented under request.natural_language_input; semantic input is represented under request.semantic_input. The request operation and the session are distinct: requests carry the current user event, while the client returns session state received from the preceding response. The Handler protocol also defines passivity as a request operation.

TDM represents text and speech input differently. Text uses a natural-language input with modality: "text" and utterance; speech uses modality: "speech" and a hypotheses array containing utterance and confidence values. However, the Pipeline version documented here reads hypotheses in its normal neural path for natural-language input, so the text shape is not verified end-to-end for that revision. Handler tests that mock the Pipeline do not establish otherwise. Verify text integration against the coordinated deployed revisions.

The offer_id in the route identifies the offer for a new session. An existing session.offer_id takes precedence over the route value. On session start, the Handler associates the selected offer with the session if no offer ID is already present. Start a new conversation with a fresh session object; do not reuse a session to switch offers. Continue a session by returning its response session with the next request. The Pipeline initializes session history and IDs, while TDM initializes the information state.

The optional non_neural query parameter is passed as a request modifier. If the session does not already specify neural, a truthy parameter value sets session.neural to false; otherwise the Handler defaults it to true. Do not send the string false expecting it to be interpreted as Boolean false.

docs.title: Response and turn-taking
docs.text:
The response carries output, session, and, where relevant, context. output.moves describes the dialogue moves; output.utterance carries realized text when present. output.expected_passivity tells the client when to send a passivity request. The Handler may adjust passivity and speech completion timing, so client behavior should follow the response fields rather than hard-code a timeout; expected_passivity may be null when passivity timing is disabled.

The Handler adds a request ID when one is absent and propagates it through the request/session. Preserve the returned session as an opaque state object; applications should not edit DME-owned session fields.

docs.title: Session privacy
docs.text: The documented Handler implementation encrypts non-whitelisted session fields into session.encrypted_data on ordinary session-bearing responses. The SESSION_ENCRYPTION_KEY setting is required; there is no plaintext fallback when it is missing. encrypted_data is a dictionary mapping each session field name to an encrypted JSON value, not one encrypted session blob. Keep the same key available while clients may resume sessions created with it. The Handler decrypts these values on the next request and merges them back into the session. Plaintext values take precedence if the same key appears in both places. Clients must round-trip session.encrypted_data unchanged and must not log or expose session contents. This mechanism does not authenticate the plaintext fields as a whole session object.

docs.title: Pipeline hand-off and service calls
docs.text: The Handler forwards interaction requests to the Pipeline. The Pipeline can return a service-call request instead of a final output; the Handler invokes the requested HTTP service, attaches its result, and calls the Pipeline again. However, the Handler/Pipeline/TDM versions cited in Architecture do not establish a working end-to-end continuation contract for every operation: Handler action and validator results are placed in request.query_results, while TDM's schema defines separate action_results and validation_results; Pipeline also expects a service-result event marker that Handler does not add. Verify and align all three revisions before relying on action or validator continuation. The generic round-trip description is not proof of compatibility between deployments.

docs.title: Response variants and compatibility
docs.text: Wakeword handling occurs within the registered interaction route and can produce a no_content response without output or session. Other legitimate response variants include output.actions such as EndSession and structured HTTP errors. Handler error responses use an error array with fields such as id, status, title, and detail (and may include code). Clients should handle these separately from a normal completed turn. Confirm details against the deployed Handler version.

docs.title: Pipeline API and orchestration
docs.text: The Pipeline is the service-to-service HTTP boundary called by the Handler. Its Azure Function route is pipeline-fn; with the default Azure Functions route prefix, the direct-host path is /api/pipeline-fn. The configured PIPELINE_ENDPOINT must contain the complete URL (the code also accepts the TDM_ENDPOINT fallback). A reverse proxy may expose another path. The request body uses the same versioned interaction envelope that the Handler receives; the Pipeline adds and propagates a request ID and prepares the session before processing.

docs.title: Processing sequence
docs.text:
At a high level, the current implementation:

  1. Prepares the session and neural settings.
  2. Starts interpretation and dialogue processing.
  3. May correct the leading speech hypothesis through ASR/NDU and restart interpretation if the correction changes the utterance.
  4. Ensures the final interpretation and dialogue are present in the response.
  5. Enriches the DME output and trims dialogue history.

Individual NLU, NDU, DME, NDG, and VOG HTTP calls are conditional. Their endpoints are configured through FUNCTION_ENDPOINT_* application settings; for example, FUNCTION_ENDPOINT_DM, FUNCTION_ENDPOINT_NLU, FUNCTION_ENDPOINT_NDU, FUNCTION_ENDPOINT_NDG, and FUNCTION_ENDPOINT_VOG. Optional paths include ASR-NDU, AB-NDU, Q&A NDG, and system NDG. NLG is different: Pipeline invokes Tala's authored NLG realization in-process, not through a FUNCTION_ENDPOINT_NLG. See pipeline/endpoints.py in the Pipeline repository for the complete current HTTP endpoint list.

The Pipeline version documented here fills missing neural settings and model selectors from deployment settings/defaults, but existing truthy session values take precedence. Resolved values therefore persist across turns and can outlive a deployment configuration change. The Handler's non_neural query parameter only sets session.neural=false when that field is absent; it does not override an existing or offer-supplied value. Non-neural mode also does not guarantee that no NDG HTTP request is made. Verify actual feature flags and downstream behavior against the deployed revisions.

The defaults in that Pipeline version for session.neural_settings are:

Setting Default move_ndu true asr_ndu true word_lookup_ndg true background_qna_ndg true limited_gpt_qna_ndg true generate_rb_q_feedback_ndg true select_comments_neurally false

For neural turns, model selectors use an existing truthy session value first, then the deployment setting, then the code default. Its deployment settings include GPT_MODEL_NDU, GPT_MODEL_FULLTEXT_NDU, GPT_MODEL_ASR_NDU, GPT_MODEL_NDG, GPT_MODEL_NDG_NON_STREAMING, and NDG_AZURE_OPENAI_RESOURCE. The resolved values appear in session fields model_name_ndu, model_name_fulltext_ndu, model_name_asr_ndu, model_name_ndg_non_streaming, and model_ndg.{deployment,azure_openai_resource}. Defaults and available deployment names are revision- and environment-specific.

docs.title: Request and response responsibilities
docs.text:
The Pipeline consumes JSON and returns a JSON response. Its internal PipelineRequest and PipelineResponse wrappers normalize access to the request, session, response, and request ID; they are implementation details, not separate wire formats.

Some responses represent an outstanding service invocation and do not yet contain output. The Handler owns the HTTP service round-trip and resubmits the result to the Pipeline. In the Handler/Pipeline/TDM versions cited in Architecture, Handler action/validator result keys do not match TDM's request schema, and Handler's continuation does not add the event marker Pipeline uses to recognize service results. Verify these revisions as a coordinated set before relying on action/validator continuation. Do not treat every Pipeline response as a completed turn.

docs.title: Errors and deployment boundary
docs.text:
The Azure Function entry point returns Pipeline response JSON on success. Recognized invalid dialogue domains return HTTP 400; unhandled exceptions are logged and returned as an HTTP 500 error object.

This endpoint is an internal production interface called by the Handler. Its presence in the codebase does not make it a supported standalone customer API. Coordinate wire-format changes across the Handler and Pipeline and validate them with their request/response tests.

docs.title: DDD authoring and runtime data
docs.text:
This reference uses Tala 31.0.2 as the DDD language baseline. Start with the task you need to do:

Developer task Start here Understand the DDD component model DDD source formats Choose or inspect the source syntax Domain XML · DDD JSON Define goals and dialogue flow Domain declarations · Plan items Define typed vocabulary Ontology XML Connect goals to application operations Service Interface XML Read or produce semantic expressions Semantic expressions and moves Understand persisted dialogue state DME information state

The runtime uses related but distinct representations:

Representation Purpose DDD XML / DDD JSON Definition sources for domain, ontology, and service interface. Semantic expressions Compact syntax for propositions, questions, goals, and moves. Interaction JSON Handler/Pipeline request and response envelope. TIS JSON / JSON:API Persisted and transferred DME information state. ODB Runtime offer data used to load DDDs and dialogue settings.

Do not confuse DDD JSON with JSON:API serialization of compiled model objects, or either of those with the interaction envelope. See the runtime architecture and the Handler/Pipeline references for the request path.

docs.title: DDD JSON
docs.text: DDD JSON supports a bundle or separate component files. Component objects use explicit names and arrays rather than XML attribute bags.

docs.title: Bundle and component roots
docs.text:
A bundle can be unwrapped or wrapped by a ddd key:

{
  "schema_version": "1.0",
  "ontology": {
    "name": "RoomBookingOntology",
    "sorts": [{"name": "room_type"}],
    "predicates": [{"name": "room_date", "sort": "datetime"}],
    "individuals": [],
    "actions": ["book_room"]
  },
  "domain": {
    "name": "RoomBookingDomain",
    "plans": [{
      "goal": {"perform": {"action": "book_room"}},
      "content": [
        {"findout": {"question": {"wh": {"predicate": "room_date"}}}},
        {"invoke_service_action": {"name": "BookRoom"}}
      ],
      "downdate_conditions": [{
        "in_beliefs_or_commitments": {
          "service_action_terminated": {"name": "BookRoom"}
        }
      }]
    }]
  },
  "service_interface": {
    "actions": [{
      "name": "BookRoom",
      "target": {"http": {"endpoint": "https://service.example/book-room"}},
      "parameters": [{"predicate": "room_date"}],
      "failure_reasons": ["unavailable"]
    }],
    "queries": [],
    "validators": []
  }
}

Each component may be stored separately with a root key: ontology, domain, or service_interface. Tala's ddd.config.json selects a bundle via ddd_bundle, or component files via ddd_files; ddd_bundle takes precedence when both settings are present.

docs.title: Domain JSON concepts
docs.text:
The domain object contains ordered plans. A plan has a goal and ordered content array, and may have postplan where allowed. The JSON schema and compiler accept postplans on both perform and resolve goals, despite older descriptive guidance that suggests resolve goals only. Runtime execution still depends on the goal-completion path (see Plans and postplans). Goals use {"perform": {"action": "..."}} or {"resolve": {"question": ...}}. Questions use tagged objects such as wh, yn, kpq, or alt. A condition and each plan item use a single-key object, for example {"not": {...}} or {"findout": {...}}.

downdate_conditions is the JSON spelling for explicit plan downdating. The downdate_plan field remains in the JSON schema for compatibility but does not create implicit DME downdating.

The compiler has a limitation for non-WH question types on domain queries: the JSON-to-XML conversion writes type, while XML compilation reads question_type. WH queries use the default and work as expected; do not rely on other query question types without verifying the compiled result.

docs.title: Validation and loading
docs.text:
The Draft 2020-12 DDD JSON schemas are under tala/ddd/schemas/json/. Tests check the schemas against real fixtures and test bundle wrappers. DDDJSONCompiler converts DDD JSON to XML and passes it through the XML compiler; schema validity alone is not a substitute for compiler/loader tests.

The compiler also retains an XML-shaped structural JSON form using keys such as @, attrs, children, and items. Prefer the named component format for new DDDs; use structural JSON only when maintaining data that already depends on that compatibility form.

# From the Tala repository root:
source ~/python_3_11_environment/bin/activate
pytest tala/ddd/test/test_ddd_json_schemas.py
pytest tala/ddd/test/test_ddd_json_compiler.py

Keep DDD JSON distinct from JSON:API serialization of compiled DDD model objects. JSON:API has data/included resources and is used for runtime model interchange, not as DDD definition syntax.

docs.title: DDD source formats
docs.text: Dialogue Domain Descriptions (DDDs) provide the ontology and domain rules consumed by TDM/DME, together with service-operation declarations used by plans. This reference is based on Tala 31.0.2. Its XML/JSON schemas, compiler, model code, and tests are the source of truth.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Component XML source Purpose Reference Domain domain.xml Goals, plans, conditions, questions, queries, and DDD dependencies Domain overview · Declaration index · Plan-item index Ontology ontology.xml Sorts, predicates, individuals, and actions Ontology overview Service interface service_interface.xml Service actions, queries, validators, parameters, and targets Service Interface overview

The XML components have separate roots and schemas. XSDs are provided for for domain.xml, ontology.xml, and service_interface.xml in tala/ddd/schemas/.

docs.title: XML loading
docs.text:
Tala validates and compiles the XML DDD components into model objects. Domain logic names ontology concepts, and service plan items name operations declared by the service interface. Therefore, editing one component often requires checking its references in the other components as well.

An XSD-valid document is only structurally valid. The XML compiler applies additional semantic checks; an XSD-valid document alone does not establish that a bundle loads or behaves as intended.

docs.title: DDD JSON
docs.text:
The JSON definition format uses the same component roots—domain, ontology, and service_interface—and may be stored as a bundle or in separate files. Tala's JSON compiler translates these components into the XML compiler path. See DDD JSON for structure, schema status, and examples.

DDD JSON is definition syntax. The JSON:API model representation used for compiled/runtime interchange is a different, internal serialization format.

docs.title: Domain declarations
docs.text: A DDD domain declares goals and the plans that fulfill them, along with question handling, queries, validation, and relevance relationships. Use the linked entries for construct details; the left menu lists the same references under Domain declarations.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: A goal declares an action for the system to perform or a question to resolve. See Goals.

docs.title: Plan and postplan
docs.text: These are ordered sequences of plan items for a goal and its follow-up work. See Plans and postplans and the Plan item index.

docs.title: Question parameters
docs.text: Question parameters configure question handling and incremental search. See Question parameters, Ask features, Hints, Service queries, always_relevant, and Alternative choices.

docs.title: Domain query
docs.text: Domain queries answer questions with implications, random selection, or enumeration. See Domain queries.

docs.title: Iterator
docs.text: Iterators provide named proposition sequences to the iterate plan item. See Iterators.

docs.title: Domain validator
docs.text: Domain validators declare acceptable proposition configurations. See Domain validators.

docs.title: Defaults and dependencies
docs.text: These declarations set default questions and associate dependent questions. See Default questions and dependencies.

docs.title: Source formats
docs.text: Domain declarations can be authored in Domain XML and DDD JSON.

docs.title: Domain XML reference
docs.text: Baseline: Tala 31.0.2 (tala/ddd/schemas/domain.xsd, the XML compiler, and the DDD tests). A domain describes goals and their plans, plus the queries, question parameters, iterators, validators, default questions, and dependencies used by those plans.

docs.title: Root and top-level structure
docs.text:
domain is the document root. name is required; is_super_domain is an optional Boolean. The root can contain:

Element Purpose goal A perform-action or resolve-question goal and its plan metadata. parameters Question-specific response, search, and realization settings. query Domain answers by implication, random selection, or enumeration. iterator A named enumeration consumed by an iterate plan item. validator Valid parameter configurations. default_question A question considered by default. dependency A dependency between questions. 
<domain name="RoomBooking" is_super_domain="true">
  <goal type="perform" action="book_room">
    <plan>
      <findout type="wh_question" predicate="room_date"/>
      <invoke_service_action name="BookRoom"/>
    </plan>
    <downdate_condition>
      <in_beliefs_or_commitments>
        <service_action_terminated name="BookRoom"/>
      </in_beliefs_or_commitments>
    </downdate_condition>
  </goal>
</domain>

The example assumes that book_room is an ontology action, room_date is an ontology predicate, and BookRoom is declared in the service interface.

docs.title: Goals and questions
docs.text:
The compiler requires goal/@type: perform or resolve. A perform goal names an ontology action. A resolve goal names a question. The schema's question types are goal, wh_question, kpq, alt_question, and yn_question; the question's predicate/proposition must be compatible with the ontology.

The schema permits goal children for plan, postcond, explicit downdate_condition, postplan, proposition, preferred, and superaction. Use explicit downdate_condition elements for current plan-completion semantics; the XML compiler does not process postcond.

docs.title: Plans and plan items
docs.text:
Plan items are interpreted in document order. The XML schema recognizes:

forget, forget_shared, forget_all, log, greet, invoke_service_query, invoke_domain_query, findout, raise, bind, invoke_service_action, get_done, assume_issue, assume_shared, assume_system_belief, inform, if, once, jumpto, signal_action_completion, signal_action_failure, end_turn, reset_domain_query, iterate, and change_ddd.

if contains one condition and optional then/else plans. once contains plan items and supports an optional id. findout, raise, service/domain queries, and several other items refer to the question language above; their individual XML attributes are defined in domain.xsd and compiled by tala/ddd/ddd_xml_compiler.py.

docs.title: Conditions and downdating
docs.text:
Condition expressions include and, or, not, has_value, has_shared_value, has_private_value, in_shared_commitments, in_private_beliefs, in_beliefs_or_commitments, and has_more_items. and/or contain one or more child conditions; not contains exactly one.

The in_* forms accept either predicate/value attributes or one child proposition. Child forms include predicate propositions, perform/resolve goals, service-action started/terminated propositions, action/question status, resolvedness, and knowledge-precondition propositions. For example:

<in_beliefs_or_commitments>
  <service_action_terminated name="BookRoom"/>
</in_beliefs_or_commitments>

service_action_terminated means the service call has terminated; it does not indicate success. TDM stores the proposition in shared commitments or private beliefs depending on postconfirmation, which is why in_beliefs_or_commitments can be useful in a downdate condition.

Compatibility detail: domain.xsd declares invoke_service_action/@downdate_plan with an XSD default of true, but the XML compiler defaults a missing attribute to false, and the DDD model no longer derives implicit downdate conditions from it. Do not use this attribute to end a plan; specify an explicit downdate_condition. Tala tests cover the no-implicit-downdate rule.

docs.title: Queries and question parameters
docs.text:
A domain query declares a predicate and one of three forms: one or more implications, select_at_random, or enumerate. An iterator wraps an enumeration and can set randomize and limit. has_more_items checks either a predicate-backed query or a named iterator.

Question parameters configure options including source, incremental, verbalize, always_ground, allow_goal_accommodation, hit limits, zero-hit/too-many-hit actions, service queries, alternatives, ask-features, hints, and always-relevant behavior. The complete field/child contract is in domain.xsd. <background> is not part of the domain schema; do not use it in new DDDs.

docs.title: DME information state
docs.text: The Dialogue Management Engine (DME) maintains a Total Information State (TIS) while processing a session. It contains shared dialogue state and private engine state; it is runtime state, not a DDD or an application-owned object.

docs.title: Main structure
docs.text:
The current TDM model has shared and private parts. Shared state includes previous moves, the latest utterance and turn content, questions under discussion (QUD), active goals, commitments, and a previous goal. Private state includes the agenda, beliefs, issues being accommodated, iterators, question hints, the next-move queue, the active plan, and temporary data.

The exact structure is defined by TDM's tdm/dm/tis.py model and its serialization code. Changes to state fields can affect persistence and session compatibility; coordinate such changes with the Handler and Pipeline revisions.

docs.title: Serialization and storage
docs.text:
TDM exposes JSON:API serialization for its state resources and also serializes the TIS as JSON for persistence. The CouchDB session retriever stores this serialized TIS with the TDM session record and returns a compressed serialized form to the caller. The Pipeline and Handler also carry session fields across interaction requests; that outer session envelope is distinct from the TIS serialization itself.

Use the versioned state contract when changing this format. Do not hand-edit persisted production session state based only on an example from the documentation.

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text: The Handler response session is the application round-trip object. It can contain offer data, request metadata, dialogue history, and other fields in addition to DME state. The Handler can encrypt non-whitelisted session values under session.encrypted_data. Neither that wrapper nor the encrypted values should be confused with the TIS's own JSON/JSON:API representation.

docs.title: Ontology XML reference
docs.text: Baseline: Tala 31.0.2. An ontology gives domain plans and semantic interpretations their typed vocabulary: sorts, predicates, individuals, and actions.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
ontology is the document root and requires a name. It can contain any number of these declarations:

<ontology name="RoomBookingOntology">
  <sort name="room_type"/>
  <predicate name="room_date" sort="datetime"/>
  <predicate name="selected_room" sort="room_type" multiple_instances="false"/>
  <individual name="single" sort="room_type"/>
  <action name="book_room"/>
</ontology>
Declaration Required attributes Optional attributes sort name dynamic predicate name, sort feature_of, multiple_instances individual name, sort — action name —

Built-in sort names are boolean, integer, datetime, real, string, image, domain, webview, and person_name. Declare application-specific sorts in the ontology; declaration order does not matter. An undeclared referenced custom sort is added as a static sort with a warning, so declare custom sorts explicitly. The compiler's fallback behavior avoids rejecting the document immediately but may hide a missing declaration. XML Boolean attributes use lowercase true/false.

docs.title: Sorts and individuals
docs.text:
A sort is the ontology's value type. Custom sorts can be marked dynamic="true" when the running domain must introduce individuals not declared as static entries. Individuals pair a name with a sort. Ontology loading checks individual name syntax and sort membership; sort-specific normalization occurs when semantic individuals are constructed from values. Dynamic sorts accept supplied values without that normalization.

<sort name="room_type"/>
<sort name="album_name" dynamic="true"/>
<individual name="single" sort="room_type"/>

integer, real, boolean, datetime, and person_name have corresponding Tala value normalization. image, webview, and domain are also built-in sorts; inspect their semantic model when defining values for those types.

docs.title: Predicates and actions
docs.text:
A predicate names a property and the sort of its value. feature_of associates a predicate with a parent predicate, as used by question-feature behavior. multiple_instances="true" allows multiple values for the predicate in domains that need a set of alternatives.

<predicate name="selected_room" sort="room_type" multiple_instances="true"/>
<predicate name="room_capacity" sort="integer" feature_of="selected_room"/>
<action name="book_room"/>

Predicate names are used in proposition expressions and DDD question/condition elements. Action names are used by perform goals and service invocations. A service-interface operation name (for example BookRoom) is a separate name; declare the semantic action (book_room) and service operation independently.

docs.title: References and validation
docs.text:
Domain goals and propositions refer to ontology action and predicate names. Tala compiles the ontology first and uses it while compiling the domain, so unknown names or incompatible values can fail DDD loading even when XML is well-formed.

  • Structure: tala/ddd/schemas/ontology.xsd
  • DDD JSON schema: tala/ddd/schemas/json/ontology.schema.json
  • Compiler/model: tala/ddd/ddd_xml_compiler.py, tala/model/ontology.py, tala/model/sort.py, and tala/model/predicate.py

docs.title: Questions and assumed facts
docs.text: Plan item Use assume_issue Open an issue as if the user had asked it. assume_shared Add a proposition to shared commitments. assume_system_belief Add a proposition to private beliefs. findout Ask for or resolve an answer to a question. inform Make a proposition privately available and request that it be communicated. raise Raise a question issue without making it a findout step. bind Accept relevant answers to an unasked question.

docs.title: Forgetting state and requesting user actions
docs.text: Plan item Use forget Remove facts from beliefs and commitments. forget_all Clear current beliefs and commitments, then put the top goal back on the goals stack. forget_shared Remove facts from shared commitments only. get_done Ask the user to perform an action.

docs.title: Branching and sequencing
docs.text: Plan item Use change_ddd Change the active DDD. if Select a branch by evaluating a condition. jumpto Target another goal in the active DDD. once Run a wrapped plan sequence once for a marker.

docs.title: Queries, iterators, and actions
docs.text: Plan item Use invoke_domain_query Resolve a question from a DDD domain query. invoke_service_action Invoke a Service Interface action. invoke_service_query Resolve a question using a Service Interface query. iterate Assume the next proposition from an iterator. reset_domain_query Restart a domain-query enumeration.

docs.title: Turn-taking and diagnostics
docs.text:
Plan item Use end_turn Explicitly hand the turn back to the client/user. greet Request a greeting move. log Write a diagnostic log message. signal_action_completion Complete a perform goal and stop its remaining plan. signal_action_failure Mark an action as failed.

Conditions are expressions used by if and goal completion; see Conditions and Downdate conditions.

docs.title: DDD JSON
docs.text: Each DDD JSON plan item uses a single-key object. For example, {"forget": {"predicate": "colour"}}. See DDD JSON for the bundle structure and examples.

docs.title: Semantic expressions, moves, and interpretations
docs.text: Baseline: Tala 31.0.2. Tala models dialogue semantics as typed objects and converts them to and from JSON. Semantic expressions are a compact textual notation for propositions, questions, goals, and moves in DDDs and interaction data. The parser is tala/ddd/parser.py; model encoders/decoders live in tala/model/.

docs.title: Interpretation JSON
docs.text:
Tala's Interpretation model reads an interpretation object with modality, moves, and, when required by the modality, utterance. Each move carries a semantic-expression string; the DME later parses that expression into a typed user-move object and checks that it is a move. perception_confidence is optional. Supported modalities and whether they require utterance text are defined by Tala's Modality model.

An interaction request can supply interpretations as request.semantic_input.interpretations. Alternatively, speech input arrives as request.natural_language_input.hypotheses and the Pipeline adds interpretations during processing.

An interpretation's moves are structured move objects. A user move includes semantic_expression, perception_confidence, and understanding_confidence; a DDD-specific move also includes ddd. The interpretation includes modality, moves, and (for text/speech modalities) utterance. Supported modalities are text, speech, haptic, and other; text and speech require utterance text.

docs.title: Core expression forms
docs.text:
These forms are exercised by Tala's parser tests:

Meaning Expression Predicate proposition dest_city(paris) Nullary proposition need_visa() Perform goal perform(book_room) Resolve goal resolve(?X.dest_city(X)) Proposition about a perform goal goal(perform(book_room)) Proposition about a resolve goal goal(resolve(?X.dest_city(X))) User requests an action request(book_room) Ask a wh-question ask(?X.dest_city(X)) Answer with a predicate/value answer(dest_city(paris)) Positive grounding of a proposition icm:und*pos:USR*dest_city(paris) Service action has terminated service_action_terminated(BookRoom)

Question expressions use a typed variable form such as ?X.predicate(X) for a wh-question. The parser also supports yes/no, alternative, knowledge precondition, and nested goal questions. Proposition arguments are interpreted using the active DDD ontology, so names and values are not untyped free text.

docs.title: Semantic object families
docs.text:
The model layer represents propositions, questions, goals, actions, predicates, individuals, and sets, along with user/system moves. These are structured objects, not arbitrary strings. Their JSON representation is implemented by the relevant as_dict methods and the semantic-expression parser in Tala.

ICMs (interaction control moves) include perception (per), acceptance (acc), semantic grounding (sem), understanding (und), and structure control moves such as reraise, accommodate, resume, report_inference, and loadplan. Polarity and any semantic content are part of the move representation. For example, icm:acc*neg:issue is a negative acceptance of an issue. cardinal_sequencing carries an integer step. Use Tala's ICM.create(...) and parser/model tests to check valid type/content combinations.

docs.title: Source of truth
docs.text: Use Tala's tala/model/ classes and parser tests as the serialization source of truth. This notation describes semantic objects; it does not define which understanding or realization service produces them.

docs.title: Service Interface XML reference
docs.text: Baseline: Tala 31.0.2. The service interface declares operations referenced by domain plan items and binds them to parameters and transport targets.

docs.title: Operations and required structure
docs.text:
The root <service_interface> contains action, query, and validator declarations. An action has this structure:

<service_interface>
  <action name="BookRoom">
    <parameters>
      <parameter predicate="room_date" format="value"/>
      <parameter predicate="selected_room" optional="true"/>
    </parameters>
    <failure_reasons>
      <failure_reason name="unavailable"/>
    </failure_reasons>
    <target>
      <http endpoint="https://service.example/book-room"/>
    </target>
  </action>
  <query name="available_room">
    <parameters>
      <parameter predicate="room_date"/>
    </parameters>
    <target>
      <http endpoint="https://service.example/find-rooms"/>
    </target>
  </query>
</service_interface>

The example endpoint is illustrative only; deployed endpoint values belong in service configuration.

Operation Required children Accepted target forms action parameters, failure_reasons, target <frontend/> or <http endpoint="..."/> query parameters, target <http endpoint="..."/> validator parameters, target <http endpoint="..."/>

Operation names must be unique within their type. A target is required. Query and validator frontend targets are rejected by Tala's XML compiler tests.

For an action, keep the <parameters>, <failure_reasons>, and <target> children even when a section is empty. An empty failure list is written as <failure_reasons/>. Queries and validators do not have a failure_reasons child in the XML format.

docs.title: Parameters and results
docs.text:
Each <parameter> requires an ontology predicate. Its optional format is value or grammar_entry; optional is an XML Boolean. For HTTP targets the service receives both the semantic value and the language grammar entry. The format selector chooses the frontend representation for frontend-targeted actions.

HTTP actions may declare failure_reason names. Frontend-targeted actions must have an empty <failure_reasons/> section; the compiler rejects named frontend failure reasons while loading the Service Interface. For HTTP actions, the runtime does not enforce that an empty declaration means the operation always succeeds. The action result and any declared failure information are consumed by TDM's service-action execution and reporting logic.

Parameter attribute Values Meaning predicate Required ontology predicate Selects the argument to bind and pass to the target. optional XML Boolean Marks the argument optional. format value or grammar_entry Selects the frontend argument form. HTTP targets receive both representations.

For queries, name must match the ontology predicate of the question passed to the service. The runtime looks up and sends that predicate name; a domain service_query mapping selects a question rather than creating an operation alias.

frontend delegates actions to the application-facing side. http invokes the declared HTTP endpoint; query and validator operations use this target.

docs.title: Compatibility boundaries
docs.text:
The XSD declares an entity_recognizer element, but the ServiceInterfaceCompiler builds only actions, queries, and validators. Do not assume an entity-recognizer declaration is part of the runtime ServiceInterface model.

The DDD JSON schema uses a shared target shape that permits a frontend target for all operation types. The XML compiler rejects frontend targets for queries and validators after JSON is converted to XML. Use HTTP targets for those operations and compile/load the bundle to validate it.

docs.title: Alternative choices
docs.text: An <alt> child contributes one choice to an alternative question. Depending on the question, the choice can be a proposition, a resolve goal, or a perform goal.

docs.title: Use in a question
docs.text:
Place one or more alt children in an alt_question supplied to findout or raise:

<findout type="alt_question">
  <alt><resolve type="wh_question" predicate="monthly_payment"/></alt>
  <alt><resolve type="wh_question" predicate="interest_rate"/></alt>
</findout>

Resolve/perform alternatives let the user choose which question or action to pursue, for example:

<raise type="alt_question">
  <alt><perform action="book_train_ticket"/></alt>
  <alt><resolve type="wh_question" predicate="train_delays"/></alt>
</raise>

docs.title: Proposition alternatives
docs.text:
For a choice among values of a proposition, use a child proposition:

<findout type="alt_question">
  <alt><proposition predicate="destination" value="chelsea"/></alt>
  <alt><proposition predicate="destination" value="fulham"/></alt>
</findout>

Question parameters can also list propositional alternatives for a question:

<parameters question_type="wh_question" predicate="minute_to_set">
  <alt><proposition predicate="minute_to_set" value="0"/></alt>
  <alt><proposition predicate="minute_to_set" value="1"/></alt>
</parameters>

The alt element has no attributes of its own. It appears as question content; it is not a plan item. See Findout, raise, and Question parameters.

docs.title: Bind
docs.text: XML element: a plan item declaring a question that can be answered or accommodated from user input, but which the plan does not ask the user to answer. It is commonly used for optional parameters.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
<bind type="wh_question" predicate="price_class"/>

type and predicate describe the question using the same question model as findout. The default type is wh_question. A bind can contain the same question children supported by the shared question XML structure, including alt and embedded_question where appropriate.

bind can appear in a goal plan, postplan, or an if branch. Its question content can be supplied by type/predicate attributes or by the question children described in Findout: proposition, perform, resolve, alt, or embedded_question.

Attribute Type Default Meaning allow_binding_yn_answers Boolean false Allows relevant yes/no answers to bind to a yes/no question in the active plan.

The compiler rejects allow_binding_yn_answers="true" unless the bind question is yes/no. DDD JSON has the same Boolean option; compilation rejects the flag on a non-yes/no question there as well.

docs.title: Behavior and placement
docs.text:
A bind does not produce a question prompt. It lets TDM consider a relevant user answer for the bound question while the bind remains in the active plan. When the DME executes the bind plan item, it removes it from the plan. Place a bind after plan items that need it—usually at the end of the plan—or it can be removed before later steps can consume an answer.

The DME considers compatible user propositions for questions still present in the plan. Yes/no answers are excluded unless a matching yes/no bind explicitly sets allow_binding_yn_answers="true".

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Optional WH parameter:

<plan>
  <findout type="wh_question" predicate="destination"/>
  <bind type="wh_question" predicate="price_class"/>
</plan>

Yes/no bind:

<bind type="yn_question" predicate="need_visa"
      allow_binding_yn_answers="true"/>

DDD JSON:

{
  "bind": {
    "question": {"yn": {"predicate": "need_visa"}},
    "allow_binding_yn_answers": true
  }
}

See domain XML and DDD JSON.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text: Conditions are expressions evaluated against the Total Information State (TIS). They appear in if plan items and inside a goal's downdate_condition.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
<has_value predicate="p"/>
<has_shared_value predicate="p"/>
<has_private_value predicate="p"/>
<in_shared_commitments predicate="p" value="x"/>
<in_private_beliefs predicate="p" value="x"/>
<in_beliefs_or_commitments predicate="p" value="x"/>
<has_more_items predicate="p"/>
<has_more_items iterator="i"/>
<and>
  <has_value predicate="p"/>
  <not><in_private_beliefs predicate="p" value="x"/></not>
</and>

Conditions can be nested inside other conditions. They do not have standalone effects: they select an if branch or determine whether a goal may be downdated.

docs.title: Condition forms
docs.text:
Form True when has_value The predicate occurs in shared commitments or private beliefs. has_shared_value The predicate occurs in shared commitments. has_private_value The predicate occurs in private beliefs. in_shared_commitments The specified proposition is in shared commitments. in_private_beliefs The specified proposition is in private beliefs. in_beliefs_or_commitments The specified proposition is in either store. has_more_items A domain query enumeration or named iterator has more items. and, or, not Boolean combinations of nested condition expressions.

The XML attributes are:

Attribute Applies to Meaning predicate has_*_value; attribute form of in_*; predicate-form has_more_items Ontology predicate whose fact/value is checked. value Attribute form of in_* Individual value. Omit it only for a nullary predicate. iterator Iterator-form has_more_items Iterator whose remaining values are checked.

has_value, has_shared_value, and has_private_value require a predicate attribute. For in_*, predicate is used with the optional value attribute or a child proposition instead.

has_*_value tests whether a predicate has any stored value; it does not test for one particular value. For in_*, the proposition may be supplied by predicate/value attributes or as a child proposition. Child forms supported Supported child forms include predicate propositions, perform, resolve, service_action_started, service_action_terminated, action_status, question_status, resolved, and know_answer.

docs.title: Parents and children
docs.text:
• Parent expressions: if and downdate_condition.
  • and and or contain one or more condition expressions; not contains exactly one. in_* conditions contain at most one proposition child.

docs.title: Attribute and child forms
docs.text:
Attribute form for a predicate/value proposition:

<in_shared_commitments predicate="flight_status" value="late"/>

For a nullary predicate, omit value. For non-nullary predicates, provide a value of the ontology-declared sort.

Scope-specific value checks:

<has_value predicate="flight_status"/>
<has_shared_value predicate="flight_status"/>
<has_private_value predicate="flight_status"/>
<in_private_beliefs predicate="flight_status" value="late"/>
<in_beliefs_or_commitments predicate="flight_status" value="late"/>

has_value checks both shared commitments and private beliefs. The other has_*_value variants test their named store.

Child form for a service-action termination proposition:

<in_beliefs_or_commitments>
  <service_action_terminated name="BookRoom"/>
</in_beliefs_or_commitments>

Child form for a perform goal proposition:

<in_beliefs_or_commitments>
  <perform action="top"/>
</in_beliefs_or_commitments>

The service_action_terminated example checks only that the service call terminated, not whether it succeeded; see Invoke service action.

docs.title: Boolean composition
docs.text:
and and or take one or more nested conditions. not takes exactly one.

<and>
  <has_value predicate="destination"/>
  <not>
    <in_private_beliefs predicate="destination" value="paris"/>
  </not>
</and>

docs.title: DDD JSON
docs.text:
The JSON representation uses a single-key object per condition:

{
  "and": [
    {"has_value": {"predicate": "destination"}},
    {"not": {"in_private_beliefs": {"predicate": "destination", "value": "paris"}}}
  ]
}

The JSON schema and compiler also support or, in_* child propositions, has_more_items, and the other condition forms listed above.

has_more_items names either the predicate queried by a domain enumeration or the iterator:

<has_more_items predicate="possible_destination"/>
<has_more_items iterator="destination_iterator"/>

Use has_more_items in an if condition. TDM revision f555673fec31 does not handle it during downdate_condition cleanup, so direct use there may raise an exception; see Downdate conditions.

docs.title: Downdate conditions
docs.text: A downdate_condition is a child of a goal. When its condition is satisfied, TDM may retire (downdate) the goal. Downdating means removing the goal from active processing; it does not necessarily mean that the goal succeeded. Multiple conditions on one goal are alternatives: any one true condition is sufficient.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
<goal type="perform" action="book_room">
  <plan>
    <invoke_service_action name="BookRoom"/>
  </plan>
  <downdate_condition>
    <in_beliefs_or_commitments>
      <service_action_terminated name="BookRoom"/>
    </in_beliefs_or_commitments>
  </downdate_condition>
</goal>

The child of downdate_condition is a normal condition expression. It can be a predicate/value condition, an in_* proposition condition, a value test, or a Boolean composition. Each condition is evaluated against the active TIS.

docs.title: Service actions: termination is not success
docs.text:
TDM records service_action_terminated whenever an invoked service action returns, including when its result is unsuccessful. With postconfirm, the termination proposition is stored in private beliefs; without it, it is stored in shared commitments. in_beliefs_or_commitments checks both locations. Therefore, this condition means “the service call ended,” not “the operation succeeded.”

The old invoke_service_action/@downdate_plan attribute does not create an implicit downdate condition. It is retained by the XML/JSON models for compatibility; author an explicit condition for current behavior.

docs.title: Downdate and cleanup behavior
docs.text:
TDM also downdates a perform/resolve goal when the corresponding action or question status is committed. Cleanup depends on the path: a resolve goal retired through an aborted-status/explicit-condition path may simply be removed without running its postplan or clearing condition facts. For paths that perform condition cleanup, in_* conditions identify propositions to clear from the corresponding TIS store; Boolean and/or conditions clean their satisfied branches. has_value checks predicate presence without identifying a specific proposition to remove, and not does not remove facts.

Although has_more_items is valid condition syntax and can be evaluated in an if, TDM revision f555673fec31 does not handle it during downdate cleanup and direct use as a goal downdate condition can raise an exception. Do not use it directly for downdating without verifying the target TDM revision.

The XML schema retains <postcond> as a compatibility form. New DDDs should use <downdate_condition>.

docs.title: Findout
docs.text: XML element: a question-raising plan item. A findout asks the user or invokes the configured question source to resolve its question. It differs from raise, which raises an issue without imposing the same findout plan behavior.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
<findout type="wh_question" predicate="destination"/>
Attribute Type Default Meaning type question type wh_question One of goal, wh_question, kpq, alt_question, or yn_question. predicate ontology predicate — Identifies a predicate-backed question when required by its type. allow_answer_from_pcom Boolean false Allows compatible answers from the user's previous commitments to be considered. alts_predicate ontology predicate — For a wh-question, supplies fact-backed alternatives from this predicate.

findout can be used in a goal plan, postplan, or a conditional plan. Its question form depends on type:

Type Question content goal Asks which goal/action is relevant; no predicate is needed. wh_question Uses the named predicate, e.g. predicate="destination". yn_question Uses a Boolean predicate or a proposition/goal child. alt_question Contains one or more alt children, each naming an alternative proposition or goal. kpq Contains an embedded_question describing the question whose answer is known.

docs.title: Parents and question children
docs.text:
findout may appear in a <plan>, <postplan>, or a <then>/<else> plan inside <if>. Its question content can be supplied by attributes or by child elements:

Child Use proposition Predicate proposition, commonly the content of a yes/no question. perform Perform-goal alternative, including a yes/no action question. resolve Resolve-goal alternative. alt Wraps an explicit alternative; repeat for each alternative. embedded_question The embedded question of a KPQ.

A KPQ embeds the question whose knowledge is being checked:

<findout type="kpq">
  <embedded_question type="wh_question" predicate="destination"/>
</findout>

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The DME raises the question represented by the plan item. When the DDD has question parameters, the configured domain/service query and question parameters may determine the answers or wording. allow_answer_from_pcom allows a compatible answer in the user's previous commitments to be reused; TDM applies its confidence and grounding rules before integrating that answer.

For a wh-question with alts_predicate, TDM collects positive known facts for that predicate. A single fact can be posed as a yes/no question; multiple facts can be posed as an alternative question. Define the ontology predicate with multiple_instances="true" when the domain needs to retain several values for it. A configured max_spoken_alts can limit the alternatives that are presented.

XML compatibility caveat: The XSD declares allow_answer_from_pcom as Boolean, but the XML compiler tests attribute presence rather than its value. Omit the attribute to disable reuse and use allow_answer_from_pcom="true" to enable it; do not write allow_answer_from_pcom="false" in XML. DDD JSON uses a Boolean and does not have this presence-only behavior.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
WH and yes/no questions:

<findout type="wh_question" predicate="destination"/>
<findout type="yn_question" predicate="need_visa"/>
<findout type="goal"/>

Explicit alternatives, where each alternative is a question or goal proposition:

<findout type="alt_question">
  <alt><resolve type="wh_question" predicate="monthly_payment"/></alt>
  <alt><resolve type="wh_question" predicate="interest_rate"/></alt>
</findout>

An alternative may also be a perform goal:

<findout type="yn_question">
  <perform action="call_contact_from_history"/>
</findout>

KPQ in DDD JSON uses a nested question object:

{
  "findout": {
    "question": {
      "kpq": {"question": {"wh": {"predicate": "destination"}}}
    }
  }
}

Fact-backed alternatives and prior-commitment reuse:

<findout type="wh_question" predicate="animal"
         alts_predicate="available_animal"
         allow_answer_from_pcom="true"/>

DDD JSON equivalent for a basic wh-question:

{"findout": {"question": {"wh": {"predicate": "destination"}}}}

See domain XML, DDD JSON, and Alternatives for additional alternative-question forms.

docs.title: Invoke service action
docs.text: invoke_service_action requests an action declared by the current DDD's service interface. The action's name and parameter predicates must agree with that interface and the ontology.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
<invoke_service_action name="BookRoom"
                       preconfirm="interrogative"
                       postconfirm="true"/>
Attribute Type Default Meaning name string Required Service-interface action name. preconfirm assertive or interrogative None Selects the preconfirmation behavior before invocation. postconfirm Boolean false Requests a natural-language report about the result. downdate_plan Boolean, deprecated XML schema says true; the compiler defaults a missing attribute to false Does not create implicit goal-downdate conditions.

Use lowercase XML Boolean values true and false. The downdate_plan schema/compiler default mismatch is retained here because it affects existing DDD interpretation; don't rely on that attribute for plan control.

docs.title: Execution and confirmation
docs.text:
The DME resolves the named action in the service interface, binds parameters, and issues the service call. preconfirm="interrogative" requires positive user preconfirmation before invocation. preconfirm="assertive" uses a system prereport as the confirmation step; the DME can proceed if the user does not object.

When postconfirm="true", TDM queues a report after the service result. It also queues a report when a call fails, even if postconfirmation is not requested. TDM records service_action_terminated whenever the call returns; that proposition does not indicate success. To end a goal based on service termination, write an explicit downdate condition.

docs.title: JSON form
docs.text:
{
  "invoke_service_action": {
    "name": "BookRoom",
    "preconfirm": "interrogative",
    "postconfirm": true
  }
}

The JSON model still permits downdate_plan for compatibility. New DDDs should use downdate_conditions on the goal.

docs.text:

  • XML/JSON compilation: tala/ddd/ddd_xml_compiler.py, tala/ddd/ddd_json_compiler.py
